title: array: one type only
blurb: array.array stores one C type; indexing, slicing and append work like a list.

notes.2: 'i' = signed int. Every element must be an int.
notes.3: Passing bytes b'abcdef' to typecode 'b' gives the byte values 97..102.
notes.4: Indexing returns a plain Python int (ASCII code of a).
notes.5: Slicing an array returns a new array of the same typecode.
notes.6: append adds at the end, like a list.
notes.7: index finds the first position of the value 102 (letter f).
notes.8: typecode tells which C type the array holds.

title: deque: both ends
blurb: Add and remove at the left and right end; rotate moves items around the ring.

notes.2: A deque built from a list keeps its order.
notes.3: append adds on the right end.
notes.4: appendleft adds on the left end.
notes.5: pop removes and returns the right end (6).
notes.6: popleft removes and returns the left end (7).
notes.7: extend adds each item on the right, in order.
notes.8: extendleft adds each item on the LEFT one by one, so the order is reversed: 11 goes first, then 22 in front of it, and so on.
notes.9: rotate(2) moves the last 2 items to the front. rotate(-n) goes the other way.

title: Counter: counting items
blurb: Counter is a dict that counts how often each item occurs.

notes.3: Counter counts every item of the list. Keys are the items, values are the counts.
notes.4: Reading a key gives its count. A missing key gives 0, not KeyError.
notes.5: update ADDS to existing counts (a plain dict update would replace them).
notes.6: elements() repeats each key as many times as its count.
notes.7: pop removes the key and returns its count.
notes.8: most_common(2) returns the 2 biggest counts as (item, count) pairs.

title: heappush and heappop
blurb: A heap list always keeps the smallest item at index 0.

notes.2: A heap is just a list. Start with an empty one.
notes.3: The first item is the smallest so far.
notes.4: 50 is added at the end. Its parent 20 is smaller, so it stays.
notes.5: 10 is added at index 2. Its parent (20) is bigger, so they swap: 10 moves up to the top.
notes.6: 40 is added at index 3. Its parent 50 is bigger, so they swap.
notes.7: 30 is added at index 4. Its parent 40 is bigger, so they swap.
notes.8: 60 is added at index 5. Its parent 20 is smaller, so it stays.
notes.9: heappop returns the smallest (10). The last item (60) moves to the top and sinks down until the order is right.
notes.10: Next smallest (20) comes out and the heap fixes itself again.

title: heapify, nlargest, nsmallest
blurb: heapify turns a plain list into a heap in place.

notes.2: This list is not in heap order: the parent 50 is bigger than its child 30.
notes.3: heapify rearranges the list in place so that every parent is smaller than its children. The smallest (10) is now first.
notes.4: nlargest(2, L) gives the 2 biggest items, biggest first.
notes.5: nsmallest(3, L) gives the 3 smallest items, smallest first.

title: bisect and insort
blurb: bisect only finds the position; insort inserts there and keeps the list sorted.

notes.2: The list must already be sorted. Duplicates are allowed.
notes.3: bisect_left returns the position BEFORE the existing 20s: 1. Nothing is inserted.
notes.4: bisect_right returns the position AFTER the existing 20s: 3. Nothing is inserted.
notes.5: insort inserts 25 at its sorted place (same as insort_right).
notes.6: insort_left puts the new 90 to the LEFT of the old 90.
notes.7: insort_right puts the new 90 to the RIGHT of the old 90. For plain ints you cannot tell the two apart.

title: insort_left vs insort_right
blurb: 20 and 20.0 are equal but different objects, so the side becomes visible.

notes.3: 20.0 equals 20, so it goes to the left of the existing 20.
notes.5: Here 20.0 goes to the right of the existing 20.

title: How bisect_left finds 20
blurb: Binary search: halve the range (lo..hi) until lo meets hi.

title: copy.copy: shallow copy
blurb: A shallow copy makes a new outer list but shares the inner objects.

notes.2: a is a list that holds two inner lists.
notes.3: b is a NEW outer list, but it holds the SAME two inner lists (#2 and #3).
notes.4: a and b are different lists, so is gives False.
notes.5: The inner list a[0] is the very same object as b[0]: True.
notes.6: Changing the shared inner list through a also changes what b sees.
notes.7: b shows 99 too because it shares the inner list.

title: copy.deepcopy: recursive copy
blurb: A deep copy duplicates the list and every nested list or object.

notes.3: deepcopy builds new inner lists (#3 and #4) as well.
notes.4: a[0] and c[0] are different objects: False.

title: deepcopy of objects
blurb: Objects of your own classes are copied too, so the copies are independent.

notes.2: Three Person objects in a list.
notes.3: deepcopy creates three NEW Person objects.
notes.4: The first persons are different objects: False (the PDF shows two different id values).
